To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the spatial compatibility effect is eliminated when stimulus location is irrelevant on half of the mixed-trial trials, but the compatibility effect is unaffected or enhanced for verbal stimuli or responses.

mixing trials that require spatially compatible and incompatible mappings of stimulus locations to response keys eliminates the SRC effect for physical location stimuli, enhances the SRC effect for verbal location stimuli, and enhances the SRC effect regardless of stimulus type when vocal responses are used.
the SRC effect is enhanced when the stimulus is a word and is reversed when the stimulus is an arrow, relative to the effect when the stimulus is its physical location.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of verbal coding in stimulus—response compatibility and the influence of trial type mixing on the compatibility effect.
the role of the stimulus in determining whether the stimulus-response compatibility (SRC) effects are observed.
the influence of the mode of stimulus presentation on the magnitude of the stimulus-response compatibility effect.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

mixing location-irrelevant with location-relevant trials eliminates the spatial compatibility effect only when the location information is conveyed by physical locations, but not by other stimulus modes.

mixing location-relevant and location-irrelevant trials does not eliminate spatial compatibility effects when the stimuli or responses are not verbal, but mixing does eliminate spatial compatibility effects for physical locations when the responses are verbal.
the SRC effect is not eliminated when stimulus color is relevant on half the trials.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the elimination of the SRC effect for physical locations when trials are mixed is due to the fact that the irrelevant location information is not directly activated for physical locations, and this is because the irrelevant location information cannot be directly activated in the absence of a direct mapping from the stimulus to a response.
the SRC effect for physical locations mapped onto keypresses is eliminated when trial types are randomly mixed, but this effect is enhanced when stimuli or responses involve verbal processing.

the SRC effect is eliminated when stimulus location is not the task relevant stimulus dimension, and the elimination is due to the lack of activation of a direct mapping between physical location and the response.
The main takeaway from our work is that
stimulus mode is a crucial factor in understanding the influence of stimulus relevance on spatial compatibility effects.
mixing can eliminate SRC effects, but only for some stimulus modes.
the SRC effect for keypress responses is reduced by mixing, and that the extent to which it is affected depends on the stimulus mode.
